main_figure_captions: Figure 1.  Study cohorts and analysis flow. BUS-BRA patients were assigned to development or internal testing. BrEaST contributed external test patients with a primary lesion mask. Each patient contributed one image. Low-quality masks had a reference Dice coefficient below 0.70.

Figure 2.  Review scores for prompted breast ultrasound segmentation. (A) The initial box is derived from the manual contour with a 10 % margin per side and clipped to the image. Four further prompts shift the clipped box by 5 % of its width or height. (B) Frozen Segment Anything Model (SAM) ViT-B reuses one image embedding to generate one mask per prompt. (C) Method A uses one minus predicted intersection over union for the initial mask. Method B uses one minus the mean Dice between the initial and four shifted masks. Each score triggers simulated review at or above its locked cutoff. The image and masks share a display crop from BrEaST case 001 [10].

Figure 3.  Planned differences at the locked thresholds. Points show differences in proportions and horizontal bars show two-sided 95 % Newcombe confidence intervals. H1 and H2 compare BrEaST minus BUS-BRA internal testing. H3 compares B minus A in the same 16 low-quality BrEaST cases. H2 and H3 intervals are nominal. The dashed line marks zero difference.

Figure 4.  Low-quality mask detection by simulated review volume. Panels A and B show the percentage of low-quality masks detected as progressively more patients are selected in descending risk order in each test cohort. Markers identify the locked thresholds and the equal-review setting. Panel C compares detection in the same 16 low-quality external cases at the locked thresholds and at 50 reviews per method.

Figure 5.  Three shared screening misses with actual targeted CPU predictions. Rows show BrEaST case089 (A, B), case175 (C, D) and case238 (E, F) [10]. Left panels overlay the released reference contour (green) and reference-derived initial prompt (blue); right panels overlay the initial prediction captured in the CPU replay (orange). Both review scores missed these three low-quality masks at the original locked cutoffs. Predictions use the original checksum-matched SAM ViT-B weights, exact source and prompt rules. Displayed Dice values come from this replay. The maximum initial-reference-Dice difference across all six replayed cases was 9.61 × 10−5; original study scores remain in Table S9. All six replayed cases and numerical comparisons appear in Figure S6 and Table S13.

Figure S3. Complete review-budget scan. A shows actual review fractions after development-threshold transfer; B and C show external and internal low-quality detection under transferred cutoffs and equal-review ranking; D shows paired external B-minus-A detection differences. Each target was evaluated using both rules, with no selection of a favorable budget. External and internal low-quality denominators are 16 and 93. Error bars in D are nominal paired Newcombe 95 % intervals conditional on observed calibration and rankings; they do not incorporate recalibration or reranking uncertainty. Numerical values are in Table S10.

Figure S4. Patient-bootstrap sensitivity, 10,000 replicates per route. A and B show A external-minus-internal detection and review contrasts; C shows external B-minus-A detection under transferred cutoffs and equal-top50 ranking. Points and bars denote medians and descriptive percentile 95 % intervals, with original estimates identified separately. D shows the joint sign-pattern frequencies: original strict pattern (fixed>0/equal<0), opposite pattern, at least one zero contrast, or matching nonzero signs. Frequencies are empirical resampling summaries, not p-values or population probabilities. Test-only resampling cannot generate an unobserved A-only low-quality detection at the fixed cutoffs; its nonnegative support must not be used to exclude a population A advantage. The original H3 Newcombe interval is retained. Complete routes, denominators and the sign matrix are in Table S11.

Figure S5. Symmetric Kitagawa accounting at the original locked cutoffs. A shows low-quality detection and B simulated review. Rows give the overall external-minus-internal difference and its composition-associated and within-stratum-rate terms for each score. Points show original estimates; bars show nominal percentile 95 % intervals from 5,000 patient-bootstrap draws. Detection components have 4,999 valid draws; overall differences and review components have 5,000. Detection weights describe diagnostic shares among low-quality cases; review weights describe shares among all patients. The within-stratum term equals the common-weight standardized difference. These are descriptive accounting terms, not causal effects. Values and rounding details are in Table S12.

Figure S6 (A). Targeted CPU predictions for the three shared screening misses, case089, case175 and case238. Left panels show the original image with released reference (green) and initial reference-derived prompt (blue); right panels show the actual replay prediction (orange). Both A and B remain below their review cutoffs. The model checkpoint, source, float32 precision and prompt geometry match the frozen protocol. Dice labels are from the CPU replay. Table S13 reports environment details and summarizes the comparisons; all 48 full-precision values are supplied in S13_all_48_comparisons_unrounded.csv. Original scores are retained in Table S9.

Figure S6 (B). Remaining A-missed low-quality cases, case024, case105 and case222, detected by B. Colors and panel layout follow part A. All 30 captured masks across the six patients are nonempty, and all quality labels and A/B review flags match the archive. The maximum initial-reference-Dice difference is 9.61 × 10−5; the maximum over all 48 fields is 0.00143543 (case105 left-shift consistency). These are new CPU arrays; original CUDA arrays were not saved, so cross-environment pixel identity cannot be verified. No new independent patients were introduced.

posthoc_paragraphs: Methods  Frozen Segment Anything Model predictions used reference-derived, known-location boxes. Confidence and prompt-disagreement thresholds targeting 20 % review in 213 development patients were transferred to 851 internal and 252 external patients. Low quality was reference Dice <0.70. Equal-review ranking and a post hoc eight-budget analysis assessed policy dependence.

As post hoc descriptive quality-control measures, we additionally tabulated true-positive (TP), false-positive (FP), true-negative (TN) and false-negative (FN) counts, sensitivity (TP/(TP+FN)), specificity (TN/(TN+FP)), positive predictive value (PPV; TP/(TP+FP)) and negative predictive value (NPV; TN/(TN+FN)). Low-quality segmentation was the positive condition and a review flag the positive test. We used Wilson 95 % intervals for these proportions. These measures assess mask-quality screening, not diagnosis of breast cancer.

We additionally performed a post hoc exploratory stratification by dataset-reported benign/malignant classification, retaining the locked risk thresholds and Dice < 0.70 definition. BUS-BRA labels came from the official Pathology field, linked by image and patient identifiers. BrEaST labels came from Classification, linked by CaseID and verified against the selected filenames; 197 diagnoses were biopsy-confirmed and 55 were confirmed by follow-up. We report stratum counts, review fractions and detection with Wilson 95 % intervals. No stratum-specific recalibration, hypothesis test or interaction test was performed. We also audited all external low-quality cases missed by A, partitioned by the B review flag.
Post hoc policy sensitivity and diagnostic accounting

The post hoc external quality-control counts were TP=10, FP=25, TN=211 and FN=6 for A, and TP=13, FP=20, TN=216 and FN=3 for B. Specificity was 89.41 % for A and 91.53 % for B; PPV was 28.57 % and 39.39 %, and NPV was 97.24 % and 98.63 %, respectively. The complete counts and Wilson intervals are provided in Tables S6 and S7.

The findings apply to reference-informed, known-location boxes. Reader-drawn or automatically generated boxes require separate evaluation. The study used one SAM checkpoint, one image per patient and one independent external dataset; overlap with the SA-1B pretraining archive could not be determined [1]. Sixteen external low-quality masks limit detection precision, and empirical resampling does not add independent patients. The new budget, resampling and accounting analyses are post hoc; they define the scope of the operating example rather than confirming a prespecified population-level reversal.

These post hoc descriptive analyses use the unchanged locked risk thresholds and the primary reference Dice cutoff of 0.70. The positive condition is a low-quality segmentation; the positive test is a review flag. These are mask-quality screening measures, not breast-cancer diagnostic measures. Development results describe calibration data and are not independent test performance.

Classification is dataset-reported and is not uniformly histopathologically confirmed in BrEaST. These are quality-screening measures, not diagnostic sensitivity for malignancy. No hypothesis or interaction tests were performed. Complete machine-readable results also include the development strata, confusion counts and misses per 100 patients.

Post hoc calibration and sampling sensitivity
raw_id_mentions: We repeated detection analyses with reference Dice cutoffs of 0.50 and 0.80 while retaining both locked risk thresholds. We also ranked the external cases by each risk score and selected the top 50 per method, the count closest to a 20 % review fraction among 252 cases. Risk ties followed the unmodified archived patient-identifier strings in lexicographic order (for example, "1", "10", "100"), rather than numeric or zero-padded image-identifier order. This equal-review comparison used a common number of reviews in the observed external cohort; its paired interval is conditional on the observed rankings.

We used 10,000 patient-bootstrap replicates per route (seed 20261106) to separate three sources of variation: test-cohort sampling at the original cutoffs; development resampling and cutoff recalibration with the original test cohorts unchanged; and both together. Cohorts were sampled independently, with paired A/B scores and labels retained within every record. Repeated draws were retained. Equal-review ranking selected exactly 50 external draw records, ordered by descending risk, original identifier string and draw-position index. The strict original direction pattern required external B-minus-A detection above zero at transferred cutoffs and below zero at equal review; ties were reported separately. Percentile 95 % intervals are descriptive, nominal sensitivity intervals and do not replace the prespecified Newcombe intervals.

We also used symmetric Kitagawa accounting and direct standardization across dataset-reported benign/malignant strata [13]. The external-minus-internal difference was partitioned into a composition-associated term and a within-stratum-rate term. Common weights were the arithmetic mean of the two cohort weights. Detection used the diagnostic shares among low-quality masks, whereas review fractions used shares among all scored patients. We obtained nominal percentile intervals from 5,000 independently sampled cohort-level patient-bootstrap replicates (seed 20261107), recalculating all weights and rates. Undefined stratum denominators remained missing. This accounting describes the observed mixtures and does not estimate causal effects.

The strict 20 %-target direction pattern occurred in 39.61 % of fixed-cutoff test-sampling replicates, 90.40 % of development-only calibration replicates and 30.94 % of full development-and-test replicates. At least one comparison was tied in 28.08 % of full replicates. Full-resampling percentile intervals were [−39.03, +11.71] percentage points for A detection and [−12.70, −1.55] for its review fraction, in external-minus-internal order (Table S11 and Figure S4). These frequencies describe empirical resampling, not p-values or population probabilities. At the original fixed cutoffs, the absence of an observed A-only low-quality detection structurally constrains the test-sampling bootstrap difference to be nonnegative; its [0.00, +40.00] percentile interval cannot exclude a population A advantage. The original H3 Newcombe interval remains unchanged.

For A, the −6.56-point external-minus-internal review difference comprised a +0.64-point composition-associated term and a −7.20-point within-stratum-rate term. Its detection difference had corresponding terms of −1.62 and −12.23 points. For B, the review terms were +0.79 and −5.32 points, and the detection terms were −0.78 and +8.91 points (Table S12 and Figure S5). The within-stratum term equals the difference after standardization to common diagnostic weights. Detection components were defined in 4,999/5,000 replicates; one replicate had no external benign low-quality case. Overall differences and all review components had 5,000 valid replicates.
Each method selected 50 of the 252 scored cases in descending risk order. Ties followed lexicographic case identifier order. Low quality used reference Dice below 0.70.

Every sampled draw is retained, including repeat draws of the same patient; these repetitions are not independent new cases. Equal review selects exactly 50 draw records by descending risk, original identifier string, then replica index. Calibration keeps all risk ties together and chooses fewer reviews when equally close; zero-denominator detection is NA without imputation.

Duplicate draws are repeated observations of existing patients, not new cases.

Overall detection differences have 5,000 valid replicates. One draw has no external benign low-quality case, making its detection stratum rate undefined; the NA propagates to both detection components, leaving 4,999 valid component replicates. Review-fraction components and overall differences have 5,000 valid replicates. Undefined rates are not imputed even when their stratum weight is zero.
